Instruction: In WordPress and WooCommerce WPGraphQL integrations, security filters or core REST authentication hooks may emit an HTTP 403 Forbidden status code on GraphQL requests containing 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' headers for customer/subscriber accounts, even while WPGraphQL successfully resolves and returns complete valid JSON data in the body. The Next.js fetcher must inspect and return 'json.data' when present rather than discarding payloads solely based on '!res.ok'.
Why: diagnosed root cause: WordPress emitted HTTP 403 status header for customer role bearer token while returning valid viewer and customer profile data, causing Next.js fetcher to discard user session on page reload

Instruction: In WooCommerce JWT and WooGraphQL integrations, validate JWT expiration ('exp') before attaching 'auth_token' Bearer headers to GraphQL requests. Expired tokens must be cleared from cookies and dropped in favor of guest sessions, and the fetcher must retry 401/403 rejected token requests without the token to prevent WordPress from rejecting cart/catalog mutations with HTTP 403 'Internal server error'.
Why: diagnosed root cause: WordPress default JWT expiration is 5 minutes while cookie maxAge is 7 days; sending expired Bearer tokens caused WordPress to return HTTP 403 Internal server error on cart mutations

Instruction: In decoupled Next.js and WooCommerce architectures across different origins, browsers block cross-origin session cookies from persisting. When transferring users from the Next.js cart to native WooCommerce checkout, invoke the WooGraphQL 'checkout' mutation with the active 'wc_session' to convert the GraphQL cart into a native order and redirect to the generated 'checkout/order-pay/<id>/?key=...' URL, or seed direct cart URLs using '?add-to-cart=<id>&quantity=<qty>' rather than navigating to a bare '/checkout' URL which loads an empty session.
Why: diagnosed root cause: bare redirects to WooCommerce /checkout send no session cookies from localhost/cross-origin frontend, presenting users with an empty cart instead of their selected products

Instruction: When developing or configuring WordPress with Docker Compose on Windows host environments, the primary root cause of severe slowness (15s–45s page loads) is that Docker volumes were bind-mounted from the Windows host NTFS filesystem ('C:\', 'D:\'). In Windows, Docker volumes MUST be Docker named volumes ('wp_core:/var/www/html' and 'wp_db_data:/var/lib/mysql') so that core WordPress files and the MySQL database reside natively inside the Linux ext4 filesystem environment (or the project must run inside the native WSL2 filesystem '/home/<user>/...'). Previous attempts to fix slowness by tweaking database settings, OPcache sizing, or container timeouts are invalid workarounds that do not solve the root I/O translation bottleneck. Only bind-mount active development folders (such as 'wp-content/mu-plugins') while keeping the core engine in named volumes.
Why: user explicit finding and Docker community consensus: cross-OS 9P filesystem translation between Windows NTFS and Docker Linux VM is the true cause of slowness; previous database and container settings tweaks were invalid

Instruction: In WordPress Docker deployments (both standalone and WooCommerce), the official 'wordpress:latest' base image only bundles 'mysqli' and 'mysqlnd' and lacks PHP's 'pdo_mysql' extension. Plugins utilizing Laravel Capsule or Eloquent ('Illuminate\Database'), such as Persian WooCommerce ('persian-woocommerce') and Gateland, fail on 'admin_init' with 'Fatal error: Uncaught Illuminate\Database\QueryException: could not find driver' and cause WordPress to return HTTP 500 errors. Do NOT create custom Docker images just to install this extension; keep standard WordPress containers and patch them via Makefile deployment targets (e.g. 'make patch-pdo-mysql' or 'make patch-wordpress' running 'docker exec -u 0 <container> docker-php-ext-install pdo_mysql && docker exec <container> apache2ctl graceful') after the container is pulled and started.
Why: user explicit instruction: do not create custom image just to run docker-php-ext-install; deploy standard wordpress containers and include makefile targets to patch the container after deployment
